newsitem.title: USA: White House asks Supreme Court to dismiss veto suit.
newsitem.headline: White House asks Supreme Court to dismiss veto suit.

text.p: Supreme Court justices Tuesday questioned whether lawmakers seeking to overturn a new law giving the president power to veto individual spending and tax items had legal authority to plead their case in court.

Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger asked the court to dismiss the suit on technical grounds, saying the six members of Congress who filed the original suit had not proved they were harmed by the new statute.
A federal court last month struck down the so-called line item veto law as unconstitutional. President Clinton has yet to use his expanded powers.
"You are really arguing about the president's hypothetical use of an act ... in the future," Dellinger told the court. "They have no legal injury because nothing has happened."

But an attorney for the lawmakers disagreed during the 70-minute court session, saying the law gave the president unprecedented power to change laws after they had been enacted by Congress, permanently altering the legislative structure.
"What our clients are objecting to here is the act fundamentally changes the process by which laws will be made in the future," said attorney Alan Morrison.

While the arguments did address some of the broader constitutional questions at stake, the justices spent most of the time questioning both sides on the issue of standing. A ruling is due before the Supreme Court recess in early July.
Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said the president had not injured the lawmakers. "Practically, a majority of members of Congress ... have caused this injury (by passing the law), not the president."

Justice Antonin Scalia said he did not recall a previous case in which a federal officer had brought suit claiming a derogation of powers. Chief Justice William Rehnquist questioned whether the law would ever actually be exercised in the political fashion suggested by its critics.

Whether it rules in the current case or a future challenge, the Supreme Court is expected ultimately to decide whether the law passes constitutional muster. The law empowers the president to sign a spending bill and cancel specific items within five days, including appropriations, tax breaks covering 100 or fewer people and new or expanded entitlements.

Congress still has the final say. A line-item veto can be overridden by a two-thirds majority in each chamber, just as in the case of normal vetoes. Forty-three of the 50 state governors have line-item veto power over their legislatures.

Presidents of both parties had long coveted line-item veto power because it vastly expands their room for manoeuvre in budgetary matters and enables them to prune spending bills to their taste without vetoing an entire bill passed by Congress. Traditionally, all-or-nothing had been their only recourse.
The lawsuit claimed the line-item veto violated the process set out by the Constitution for Congress and the presidency on how legislation becomes law.

U.S. District Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson agreed and struck down the law April 10. He said in a 36-page ruling that the law "hands off to the president authority over fundamental legislative choices" in conflict with the separation of powers sought by America's Founding Fathers and spares Congress from making "vexing choices" over which programmes to cut."
